prompt: In a relational design, what pays for keeping every fact in exactly one place?

choices.text: Joins and a planner, at read time
choices.why: Right. They answer questions nobody listed, so the schema never has to know them.

choices.text: Cheaper disk, which makes duplicated data unnecessary
choices.why: Cheap disk argues for duplication, if anything; it is not what makes normalisation work.

choices.text: Foreign keys, which copy each fact to the tables that use it
choices.why: A foreign key points at the fact; it copies nothing.

choices.text: Transactions, which make every query fast
choices.why: Transactions protect writes; they do not answer new questions.

prompt: What is the commonest first mistake when a team designs for a NoSQL store?

choices.text: Duplicating data before measuring whether reads need it
choices.why: Duplication by design is lesson 4's tool; the mistake the section names is the opposite.

choices.text: Copying the relational schema and joining in the application
choices.why: Right. It keeps normalisation's cost and throws away the joins that paid for it.

choices.text: Choosing a store with no schema at all
choices.why: A schema exists anyway (lesson 6); the mistake is about how the data is split.

choices.text: Listing every query before creating a single collection or table
choices.why: That is the method the lesson recommends, not the mistake.

prompt: Why do the stores of this course give up joins, or make them expensive?

choices.text: Because their query languages were designed before joins were invented
choices.why: Joins are older than all three products.

choices.text: Because they keep no indexes that a join could use
choices.why: MongoDB has a full index system, lesson 7; the obstacle is elsewhere.

choices.text: Because a join across machines costs network trips per row
choices.why: Right. A store built to answer from one partition cannot also promise to combine any two on demand.

choices.text: Because a join would break eventual consistency
choices.why: Consistency is lesson 5's subject; the cost here is distance between machines.

prompt: In the shop's table of access patterns, which column decides the key the data is stored under?

choices.text: What the application already knows when it asks
choices.why: Right. A product code, a customer, an order number: the value in hand is the key.

choices.text: What it wants back
choices.why: That decides the unit stored together, not how it is found.

choices.text: The expected rate
choices.why: The rate decides how much to pay for a question, not its key.

choices.text: The order the rows come back in, newest first or not
choices.why: Order is kept inside what the key finds; it does not choose the key.

prompt: "My orders" wants a customer's orders newest first, ten at a time. How can a store answer it without sorting at read time?

choices.text: By caching the sorted answer in the application
choices.why: A cache still had to sort once, and goes stale with each order.

choices.text: By storing the rows in that order
choices.why: Right. Cassandra's clustering order is exactly this, in the next sections.

choices.text: By sorting on the order number, which grows with time anyway
choices.why: That is still a sort at read time, over all of a customer's orders.

choices.text: By reading only the latest order and following links back
choices.why: Ten reads chained one after another is the slow path, not the fix.

prompt: "Orders over 500 to review for fraud" starts from nothing the application knows. In a store that answers by key, what are the options?

choices.text: A lookup by key, since every order has an id
choices.why: The ids of the orders over 500 are exactly what nobody knows yet.

choices.text: None: such a question has to move to a relational database first
choices.why: A warehouse is one option, not the only one; a structure built in advance also works.

choices.text: A scan, or a structure built in advance
choices.why: Right. At a few times a day a scan may be acceptable; at thousands a minute it is not.

choices.text: An index on the key, which makes any condition fast
choices.why: An index on the key helps lookups by key, and the condition is on the total.

prompt: Put the start of a design by access pattern in order.
items: Write down every question the application will ask
For each, note what it already knows and what it wants back
Rank the questions by their expected rate
Choose the key and the unit that answer each one
trap: No collection or table exists until the last step.

prompt: Which of these argue for embedding a piece of data inside its parent document? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: It is read together with the parent
choices.why: Right: one read hands back both.

choices.text: Its size is bounded
choices.why: Right: an order has a handful of lines, not an unbounded list.

choices.text: It belongs to the parent and to nothing else
choices.why: Right: an order line has no life outside its order.

choices.text: Many parents share it, and it changes on its own
choices.why: That is the customer, and it argues for a reference.

choices.text: It keeps growing for as long as the parent exists
choices.why: Unbounded growth meets the 16 MB limit, as the transcript did.

prompt: Why does the order keep only the customer's e-mail, and read the rest from `customers`?

choices.text: Because MongoDB cannot nest one document inside another
choices.why: The order lines are nested documents; nesting is not the obstacle.

choices.text: Because she is shared by many orders and changes on her own
choices.why: Right. Embedding it would mean one copy per order to keep in step, lesson 4's subject.

choices.text: Because an e-mail address is the only field an index can use
choices.why: Any field can be indexed (lesson 7).

choices.text: Because a document may hold only one level of fields
choices.why: That is a Redis hash; a document can nest.

prompt: The second `$push` of a 9 MB string was refused with `BSONObj size ... is invalid`. What state is Ana's customer document in afterwards?

choices.text: It holds half of the second string, cut at the limit
choices.why: An update applies whole or not at all; nothing is cut.

choices.text: It is deleted, because it became invalid
choices.why: The last `findOne` returned it, name and city intact.

choices.text: It is moved to a second document that continues the first
choices.why: MongoDB never splits a document; that design is the application's to choose.

choices.text: Unchanged: the second push never happened
choices.why: Right. The refusal is clean, and the next write that grows it will be refused too.

prompt: A product document embeds every review, and a review takes about 2,048 bytes. About how many reviews fit before MongoDB's limit of 16 MiB (16,777,216 bytes)?
hint: Divide, and ignore the product's own fields.

prompt: A blog stores each post as a document. Most posts get a dozen comments, and a few popular ones get tens of thousands. Where should the comments go?

choices.text: Embedded in the post, since they are read with it
choices.why: Read together, yes, but not bounded: the popular posts are the ones that would hit the limit.

choices.text: In a collection of their own, each one referencing its post
choices.why: Right. An unbounded list is a reference, whatever the typical case looks like.

choices.text: Embedded, with the post split into a new document each time it fills
choices.why: Possible as a deliberate pattern, but it is the application's machinery, and the section's rule points elsewhere.

choices.text: In Redis, because MongoDB cannot hold that many small documents
choices.why: A collection holds millions of small documents without trouble.

prompt: With `PRIMARY KEY ((customer), ordered_at)` and `CLUSTERING ORDER BY (ordered_at DESC)`, what does `... WHERE customer = 'ana@example.com' LIMIT 2` return?

choices.text: Ana's two oldest orders
choices.why: DESC stores the newest first, and LIMIT takes from the top.

choices.text: Any two of Ana's orders, in no defined order
choices.why: Inside a partition the order is defined by the clustering columns.

choices.text: Ana's two newest orders
choices.why: Right: October's monitor, then September's order 1001.

choices.text: The two newest orders in the whole table
choices.why: The `WHERE` names one partition; the rest of the table is not read.

prompt: Why does Cassandra refuse `ORDER BY ordered_at DESC` without a customer in the `WHERE`?

choices.text: Because order exists only inside a partition
choices.why: Right. Sorting the whole table would mean reading all of it, which is what the refusal prevents.

choices.text: Because DESC is not allowed on a timestamp column
choices.why: The table was created with `ordered_at DESC`; the column is fine.

choices.text: Because LIMIT and ORDER BY cannot appear in the same statement
choices.why: They can, once the partition key is restricted, as the error says.

choices.text: Because the table has only one node to read from
choices.why: The same refusal happens on a hundred nodes.

prompt: Order 1014 was inserted with the same customer and the same `ordered_at` as order 1013. What did Cassandra do?
hint: Is there a row with that primary key already?

choices.text: Refused the insert with a duplicate-key error
choices.why: There was no error: Cassandra has no such check on an ordinary insert.

choices.text: Kept both rows, since the order ids differ
choices.why: `order_id` was not part of the key, so the two rows had the same identity.

choices.text: Overwrote order 1013 with 1014, silently
choices.why: Right. An insert is an upsert; the fix is a key that makes each order unique.

choices.text: Moved 1014 to the next millisecond to keep it unique
choices.why: Cassandra never changes a value you wrote.

prompt: Adding `order_id` after `ordered_at` in the primary key makes it a second ___ column, so two orders placed in the same instant are two rows.
hint: It orders rows inside the partition.

prompt: In `HGETALL cart:ana@example.com`, where is the "query"?

choices.text: In a secondary index on the customer field
choices.why: There is no field and no index; the key is all there is.

choices.text: In the key name, built from what the application knows
choices.why: Right. The application builds the name from the session's customer and asks for exactly that key.

choices.text: In the `cart:` prefix, which Redis uses to group keys into a table
choices.why: To Redis the colon is an ordinary character; there are no tables.

choices.text: In the hash's fields, which the server searches
choices.why: `HGETALL` returns every field; nothing is searched.

prompt: In the lab, `KEYS cart:*` over a million keys took about 139 ms. Why is that a problem on a production Redis?

choices.text: Because it returns the keys in a random order
choices.why: Order is not the issue; the time the server spends is.

choices.text: Because Redis runs one command at a time, so every other client waits for it
choices.why: Right. For those 139 ms no basket update and no session read is served.

choices.text: Because it deletes the keys it matches
choices.why: `KEYS` only lists them.

choices.text: Because it misses keys added while it runs
choices.why: Nothing is added while it runs, since nothing else runs at all.

prompt: `SCAN 0 MATCH cart:* COUNT 1000` answered `512` and an empty list. What does that mean?

choices.text: That there is no basket in the database
choices.why: `KEYS` and `--scan` both found one; this slice simply held none.

choices.text: That 512 baskets matched and were left out of the reply
choices.why: 512 is a cursor, not a count.

choices.text: This slice held no match; continue from 512
choices.why: Right. It ends when the cursor comes back as 0.

choices.text: That the pattern is wrong, since `MATCH` needs quotes
choices.why: The same pattern found the basket through `--scan`.

prompt: Match each of the shop's questions to the structure this lesson built for it.
hint: One structure answers none of them.

pairs.right: a partition per customer, clustered DESC
a hash under cart: and the e-mail

pairs.left: show the customer's name beside the order

prompt: A year after launch, the warehouse asks for every order in status "paid" in Cassandra. What does the access-pattern approach say this costs?

choices.text: Nothing: `ALLOW FILTERING` on the existing table answers it
choices.why: It answers by reading every partition on every node, on every request.

choices.text: A secondary sort, added to `orders_by_customer` with an `ALTER TABLE`
choices.why: The clustering order cannot be altered, and it would still be per customer.

choices.text: A new table designed for that question, filled with every order written before it existed
choices.why: Right. The new question is a new structure plus a backfill, and lesson 4 keeps the two in step.

choices.text: A join between `orders_by_customer` and a table of statuses
choices.why: Cassandra has no joins.

prompt: The shop starts needing "every open basket" on each admin page view. What does the section recommend instead of `SCAN`?

choices.text: Running `KEYS cart:*`, since there are few baskets
choices.why: `KEYS` walks every key, sessions included, however few baskets there are.

choices.text: A set of basket keys, updated with each basket, so the question has a key of its own
choices.why: Right. A question asked often gets a structure; a scan on every page view means a key is missing.

choices.text: A `SCAN` with a larger `COUNT`, so it finishes in one call
choices.why: A huge COUNT turns SCAN back into one long pause, which is KEYS again.

choices.text: Moving the sessions to another Redis so the scan has less to read
choices.why: Smaller, but still a scan on every page view.
